author: sxarsky
fponticelli
body:
Closes #145. Closes #152.

## #145 — the last three roving tab stops

`menubar`, `navigation-menu` and `tags-input` computed their tab stop inline (`focused === x ? 0 : -1`) with no fallback. Nothing prunes `focused` against the current item list, so removing or disabling the focused item left EVERY item at `tabindex="-1"` and the widget dropped out of the Tab order — the WCAG 2.1.1 failure #126 fixed for radio-group/toggle-group/tree-view/toolbar. All three now route through the shared `rovingTabStop`, memoized per update with `deriveOnceN` (so one item's tabindex does not cost a scan of the whole list, #124).

- **menubar** — `rovingTabStop(menus, disabledMenus, focused)`. Its private `firstEnabled` duplicate is dropped for the shared one.
- **tags-input** — the issue's own correction is what the tests drive: only the CHIPS lose their stop (the text input is a plain `<input>` and stays a natural tab stop), and the path that strands the index-keyed stop is `setValue`, not `removeTag` (which clears it explicitly). The stop resolves by **index** (`String(i)` — already the widget's `data-index` DOM identity, the key `focusRovingItem` uses), not by value: `unique: false` allows duplicate tag values and a value-keyed stop would hand two chips `tabindex="0"`. A null `focusedIndex` still seats no chip — that is the state `removeTag`/`clearAll` return to, meaning the roving focus is on the text input; seating a chip there would put it ahead of the input in the Tab order.
- **navigation-menu** — see below; the first revision of this PR only half-closed it.

The SCOPE note on `rovingTabStop`'s doc comment (and its twin in `roving-tab-stop.test.ts`) is removed.

### navigation-menu: the tab stop is resolved against what is TABBABLE

The first revision routed navigation-menu through `rovingTabStop` only where `state.items` is populated, and kept `focused ?? latched` for an EMPTY `items` — the documented STATIC-menu configuration. Review found two reachable zero-tab-stop states there, i.e. exactly the failure #145 exists to remove. Both are reproduced by tests in this PR.

- **Repro A** — `{...init({ items: [] }), focused: 'gone' }` with triggers `a`/`b` built: a `focused` id that no `item()` ever saw was honoured on trust, so ZERO items reported `tabindex="0"`.
- **Repro B**, on a static menu, through the machine's OWN messages with no consumer error: hover a branch → `openBranch('file')`; the submenu trigger's own `onFocus` sends `focus: 'file-open'`; the pointer leaves → `scheduleClose` → `closeAll`, and the branch's `content` gets `hidden: true`. The stop stayed on `file-open` — present and unique by the letter of the roving-tabindex pattern, and inside a `hidden` container, so the nav had **no tabbable element at all**.

**The fix.** The single-id LATCH is replaced by `rendered`, a `Map` of every id handed to `item()` → its `ancestorIds`, in call order (document order for any depth-first view). It does two jobs:

1. **Membership** for a static menu, closing Repro A — `focused` is now pruned against the ids actually rendered instead of trusted. A full list is never worse than the latch it replaces: its first entry *is* the latch, and it prunes a stale `focused` the latch could not.
2. **Visibility**, closing Repro B — a candidate whose `ancestorIds` are not all in `state.open` sits inside a `hidden` panel and is filtered out. An id `item()` never saw is taken as visible — unknown is not hidden.

   **This is new weight on an existing parameter, not a free ride on one.** `item()` has always taken `ancestorIds`, but every prior read of it sat inside an `isBranch` guard, so on a nested LEAF it was genuinely dead and omitting it cost nothing. It now decides tabbability: a consumer who omits it on a nested leaf gets the old Repro B back (`all = ['file-open']`, `tabbable = []`). Not a regression — that is the behaviour they already had — but the requirement is real, and `NavMenuParts.item`'s doc now marks it REQUIRED on nested items rather than optional.

`state.items` still wins wherever the consumer maintains it, and the visibility filter applies there too, since `items` is documented as accepting deeper ids. If the filter empties the candidate list the UNFILTERED candidates answer, so the worst case degrades to the previous behaviour rather than to no stop at all.

**`rendered` accumulates and never prunes, so only the FIRST of the latch's two defects is fixed.** `item()` is build-only and an unmount is invisible to `connect()`, so a row that goes away stays in the map: with an EMPTY `items`, the fallback can still name an id no longer in the DOM. The review measured three such zero-stop states — an `each` row removed, a `show`-gated top-level trigger switched off after being focused, and `items` still listing a gated-away id. **None is a regression** (identical on `main` and on this PR's first revision), all three are the DYNAMIC configuration the docs route to `state.items`, and that documented route demonstrably works. Fixing it would need a deregistration signal `connect()` cannot observe, so it is written down in the source next to the claim it qualifies rather than papered over.

**One visible cost of the degrade-to-unfiltered fallback**, for the record: it looks at the candidate LIST, not the DOM. `items: ['a','b']` with both inside a shut `file` branch gives `{ file: -1, a: 0, b: -1 }` — the stop sits on a hidden trigger while `file`'s own rendered, tabbable trigger reads -1, because it was never declared a candidate. Defensible for that input (the consumer named exactly two eligible ids and both are away), and it is the one place the "never worse than one untabbable stop" reasoning shows through, so it is documented rather than left to be found later.

**Alternatives ruled out, with evidence.** `rovingTabStop(items.length ? items : latched ? [latched] : [], …)` makes the existing `once an item is focused it owns the tab stop` test fail — a one-id list strips the stop from every trigger but the first. Membership *without* the ancestor filter leaves Repro B untouched (mutation M3 below reddens 3 tests). Both are pinned as mutations rather than described.

**Ordering.** The memo is keyed on the STATE inputs only and reads `rendered` from the closure — deliberately, not an oversight. `item()` runs during view construction while tabindex bindings produce during materialisation, and every authoring helper is a lazy `Mountable`, so the registry is complete before the first binding evaluates (proved by the two new live-mount integration tests, one of which asserts against the FIRST commit). Where it is not — a unit test interleaving `item()` with reads, an `each` row built after mount — every trigger in the pass still compares against ONE memoized answer, so "exactly one tab stop" holds against a half-built registry. Adding a registry revision to the memo key would trade that invariant for a freshness nothing needs.

**Accepted cost, unchanged from the first revision:** with `items` populated, a `focused` id that is not in it (a nested submenu item the consumer chose not to list) no longer owns the stop — the nav still has exactly one, and consumers who want a deeper id eligible add it to `items`.

## #152 — non-finite input

Option A as the issue prefers: one boundary check in `clamp`, so `init` is covered like every reducer. A non-finite input maps to a defined legal value — the bound `±Infinity` points at when that bound is finite (so `angle-slider`'s Home/End, which deliberately send `±Infinity`, keep working), else `finiteInRange`. `snapToStep` takes the same policy for its direct callers; it is unreachable from `clampToStep`, which clamps first. `slider`'s `withThumb` doc claim now holds with no finiteness caveat.

**`finiteInRange` is zero clamped into the range, and its doc comment now says so.** The first revision's comment claimed "`min` when it is finite (the range's own origin, matching `gridOrigin`)", which is false for every range below zero —

## The trust feature, completed

The citation `quote` was `content.slice(0,240)` — the chunk HEAD — so tapping a chip often showed a passage ending just before the cited value (2026-08-13 QA finding: the torque spec sat outside the window). Two changes on canonical seams:

**Server**
- `src/lib/quote-window.ts` — `relevantQuoteWindow(text, question)`: deterministic sentence scoring against the question's terms (digit-bearing tokens like `0.71`/`f004` count from length 2), best segment wins, head fallback when nothing matches. Zero-token per the ZTA rule. `buildCitations` now windows every quote on the question.
- **New** `GET /api/equipment-notebooks/[id]/sources/[docId]/passage?page=N` — full chunk text(s) for one source page, on demand. Session-gated; notebook/tenant **IDOR 404** via `equipment_notebook_sources`; the `knowledge_entries` read runs on the **raw pool with the hybrid law** `(is_private = false OR tenant_id = $caller)` — never `withTenantContext` (RLS would hide shared OEM rows). Read-only.
- Tests: 6 windowing (incl. the torque-miss regression) + 4 endpoint contract (hybrid-law SQL asserted, IDOR no-leak, page validation, null-page bind).

**Mobile**
- Citation sheet shows the centered quote and gains **"Show full passage"** — fetched on demand (never inlined in chat/evidence frames), scrollable per-chunk, honest loading/error/empty states. Suite 28/28, tsc clean, bundle builds.

**Post-deploy verification owed** (both changes are server-side): re-ask the torque question vs prod → quote contains `0.71`; open the full passage from the citation sheet.

author: dniachini-droid
body:
## What

Your four decisions, written into canon. **Spec, decision record and backlog only — no application code, no test, no chemistry constant.**

**1. The rails are fixed** (`reef-chemistry.md` §3). The `[user]` may **tighten** a rail clause is withdrawn. One figure per element, the same for every user; no setting either way. Resolves the same-day contradiction with `wizard-states.md` §21 in §21's favour, on §21's own reasoning. **Tighten-never-loosen is re-homed, not deleted** — it applies to §2's bands, which the user sets as tightly as they like inside safe bounds the app refuses to let them leave. §3 also now records that nothing is withdrawn in practice: `rateLimitDose` (`alkalinity.js:351-379`) reads settings only for plausibility, `safeDoseBand` (`safe-rate.js:43-48`) reads a hardcoded constant, `Setup.jsx` has no rate field. And it records the revisit path — if 0.5 dKH/day proves too fast on a real tank, §3 is where it changes, for everyone.

**2. Two vocabularies, both registered** (`wizard-states.md` §22, new). The six consistency verdicts in `reading-meaning.js` are registered, not removed and not folded into §13's seven. §13 answers *where is this reading*; §22 answers *how steady has this been over the window*. Six verdicts, seven bands, nothing else — a seventh is a finding on the same terms as an invented band. §13 and §15 cross-reference it.

**3. `drifting` → `unsettled`, plus a tier and a refusal** (§22). Canon's `drifting` is *inside* the band sliding toward an edge; the verdict fired on the median *outside* the band (`reading-meaning.js:218`). Rename only — no threshold or condition moves with it. Two rules the escalation didn't ask about, now written:
- **The alert tier.** `tone` is fixed per verdict (`:196-220`), so a lethal value and a mildly-off one both read `sliding` in the same colour. Every verdict now carries the tier of the **latest** reading's §13 band (§26 — position is the last reading), renders no calmer than it, and at the alert tier leads with the position. The verdict word doesn't change; tone and sentence order do.
- **Unknown refuses.** `consistency` initialises to `"unknown"` (`:141`) and every branch testing it fails open, so an ungradeable parameter still reaches `controlled` or `unsettled` on the median test alone. Per §13's last row it must refuse and name what is missing.

**4. One word for a notice, and the colours** (§15, §20). `notice` registered as the single term; **"Worth knowing about"**, **"Hidden notes"/"Notes"** and **"notification"** banned, and §20's confirmation sentence restated as *"This is flagged as a serious notice. Are you sure you wish to hide it?"* (TW-031 updated to quote it). §15 gains a **colour registry**: severity colours reserved and **unchanged**, no parameter brand colour byte-identical to one. **Phosphate `#C4285B` → `#9B3A8C`** (plum), **potassium `#926A09` → `#5F7A12`** (olive).

### In plain terms — what changed

Four decisions written down; the app behaves exactly as it did this morning. No knob for how fast the app may move your tank — one speed limit per parameter, the same for everyone, and the knob was only ever a promise on paper, never built. "Tighten it, never loosen it" still applies to your target ranges, where it belongs. The app has two sets of words about a parameter and now admits it: one for where your reading is, one for how steady it's been. One of the second set's words was "drifting", which on the badge next to it means nearly the opposite — it's now "unsettled". The thing the app shows you about a parameter is a **notice**, one word not four. And your phosphate chart is no longer drawn in the exact red the app uses for danger.

## Why

Two of these close live contradictions and two close a vocabulary drift, all of them raised in `.agent/needs-dan.md`:

- **Item 8** — §3 and §21, settled the same day, disagreed on whether a keeper may ask for a gentler daily limit. Resolved as option (b).
- **Item 7** — a second, home-made vocabulary sat on top of the official band words, and its one shared word meant the opposite depending on which badge you read, in the same modal. Resolved as option (a).
- **Item 6's two closable notes** — one on-screen concept shipping under three names, and two brand colours byte-identical to severity colours.

## Spec reference

- `docs/spec/reef-chemistry.md` §3 (rewritten clause), header amendment note
- `docs/spec/wizard-states.md` §22 (new), §15 (three registry rows + the colour registry), §20 (the word, and the restated confirmation), §13 and §21 (cross-references), header and Part III line

## Risk (what breaks if I'm wrong)

**Nothing breaks today** — the tree's only edits are Markdown, so no behaviour, no number and no test result moves. The risk is in what the decisions commit you to:

- **Decision 1's cost is real and is written into §3 rather than glossed:** a keeper whose corals react badly to fast swings has no path through the app at all, not even a manual one. If that turns out to be your tank, the fix is to change 0.5 dKH/day in §3 for everyone, not to add the setting back.
- **Decision 3's alert tier is the one with a livestock consequence.** If it's implemented wrong — reading the tier from the median or a fitted value instead of the last reading — a steadiness verdict could still show calm over a level that needs attention, which is the exact failure it exists to stop. §22 names §26 explicitly for that reason, and TW-045 is the checker.
- **Decision 4's colours are chosen, not merely different.** If the figures are wrong the chart could fail §18's contrast floor. They were computed, not eyeballed, and both re-derivations are in §15 (contrast 5.76:1 and 4.54:1 against a 4.5:1 text floor; CIE76 separation 37.9 and 32.7 from the severity colour each replaces; palette's tightest pair unchanged at 16.4).

**In plain terms:** none of this can hurt the tank this week, because none of it is running yet. The thing to check before approving the code is the steadiness-colour rule — if it reads your tank's position from the wrong number it will keep doing the thing you asked it to stop doing, which is showing a calm colour over a level that needs attention.

## Merged up — the run-state restructure

`main`'s run-state restructure (`a2ea1b4`, PR #42) landed while this was open and deleted the shared `.agent/run-state.md`. `origin/main` (`e3b9658`) is merged in. **One conflict, the expected one**: this branch had written to the file main deleted. Resolved per the new convention — this run's record is now `.agent/runs/2026-08-14-four-owner-decisions.md`, content carried across unchanged apart from the merge notes, and no other run's file was read into or edited by it.

**The merge also produced a silent collision, now fixed.** Git combined both branches' backlog additions cleanly and left **two TW-042s** — main's, for "`.agent/backlog.md` is the next shared-singleton conflict, surviving on luck", and this branch's notice-wording item. This branch's three renumber to **TW-043 / TW-044 / TW-045**; main's keeps TW-042, because it is merged and referenced elsewhere while these were referenced only from here. Every cross-reference in `.agent/needs-dan.md` and the run log moved with them. Worth noting the incident is a small instance of exactly what main's TW-042 warns about.

## Verification (commands run + output)

Still spec-only after the merge:

```
$ git diff --stat origin/main...HEAD -- . ':!*.md'
(empty)
```

```
$ npm ci && npm run verify
...
ALL BLOCKING CHECKS PASSED (advisory findings above, if any, are tracked in the backlog)
```

Includes `legacy-port:golden`, `legacy-port:protocols` and `legacy-port:invariants` green, which is the run worth having on a branch that touches canon.

Both advisory checks fail at **exactly the documented baseline**, unchanged by this branch:

```
$ node scripts/verify/deadcode.mjs
FAIL dead or undeclared code:
    src/components/Dashboard.jsx:298 ParamHistoryModal: 'doseAdvice' computed

author: pdlug
body:
Four mechanisms that make backend capability variance structural rather than conventional, shipped as a measured pilot with the sweep deferred to a named follow-up whose enforcement ratchet already holds the line.

**Recursive traversal as a declared capability.** `BackendCapabilities.recursiveTraversal` with a module-branded verdict — constructible only by the resolver, so an inline `{ supported: true }` literal cannot exist — threaded as a required input through all six `WITH RECURSIVE` emission sites (query traversal, subgraph, historical identity reconstruction and expansion, the identity window ledger) and a comment-stripped `(file,line)` inventory ratchet that fails in both directions on a seventh site. The weighted-shortest-path extractor gains a predecessor-walk fallback reproducing the recursive extractor's exact semantics, with the shared tie-break fragment as one owner. Absent means supported (breaking every existing external backend inside a minor is not acceptable); explicit declaration becomes a certification requirement in the conformance kit. This is the prep that makes a recursion-less engine a wrapper-sized task when its upstream ships.

**Six capability bundles, piloted by measurement.** A registry where each bundle's membership, arity, and per-operation disposition (`refuse` with a named typed error, or `fallback` to a named tested degradation) were derived by running an 81-member drop matrix against main — not asserted from names, which round-by-round measurement repeatedly proved wrong. Verdicts are data resolved once against the `GraphBackend`; member binding happens at the call site against the executing port, so a bound function can never escape a transaction; port-mismatch semantics are disposition-keyed (a refuse row's mismatch throws `BUNDLE_PORT_SURFACE_MISMATCH`, a fallback row's mismatch takes its declared fallback — a shipped degradation contract proved the blanket throw wrong). The claims verdict is a memoized lazy thunk because a landed acceptance test requires unconstrained creates to succeed on a backend whose declaration only the constrained path may refuse. A type-aware access-inventory scanner pins seven honest buckets — pilot 0, annotated residue, deferred ceiling, reasoned floor, statically-required, not-an-access, and a pinned exactly-four trusted-import exclusion — so the deferred sweep (WS5b) cannot regress silently and inherits the pilot's threading measurements as design inputs.

**Write-fence plans.** Eight call sites that each spelled the same dialect-keyed lock decision inline now consume one `resolveWriteFencePlan` (`lock` / `engine-serialized` / `unfenced`), with `requireWriteFence` as the single checker of an operation's lock requirement against the plan. Two construction gates land with it: Operational Identity refuses on an unfenced engine, and TypeGraph-owned recorded-clock allocation (`history` or `revisionTracking` — the resource is the clock row, not the option name) refuses likewise, plus an interim refusal for `recordedTimeOwnership: "engine-native"` until the engine-native read path lands. A custom backend that hosts these features without declaring `pessimisticLocks` is refused immediately — the error text carries the exact one-line declaration to add per dialect, so the refusal is the migration guide. The dialect-seam lint extensions land in the same commit as the consolidation they police, proven red-before/green-after.

**The external-consumer API-surface gate.** CI compares the generated API reports against the last published tag and fails on the three breaking shapes external consumers actually hit: a required member added to a contravariantly-reachable type, a member removed, an optional member tightened to required. The exceptions ledger is empty and audited in both directions. One documented limitation, discovered by this PR's own freeze batch: changes inside a member's value type (`Pick`/intersection bodies) are outside the checker's inventory — named in the checker's scope note and carried as a conformance-kit obligation rather than papered over.


Every batch shipped with named mutation checks recorded in its commit body, and the branch's escalation record — nine design-vs-tree conflicts caught at spec time, each resolved by a ruling against measurement rather than an improvisation — is documented in the workstream's implementation notes.

body:
## Summary
- Found via a live client-to-vendor bid/quote transaction walkthrough (real UI, real Playwright session, disposable DB): the BidBoard "Generate quote" button was always active regardless of tier-access, and `POST /api/autoquote/generate` had **no access check at all** — not even the private-bid check every other bid endpoint enforces. A vendor could preview a bid's full budget/scope before ever being permitted to act on it, including bids still inside a higher tier's exclusive window or private/invite-only bids they were never invited to.
- The actual quote-submission endpoint (`POST /api/bids/:id/quote`) already enforces `canVendorAccessBid()` correctly, so this closes the one real gap in the chain rather than touching working enforcement.
- `server/src/routes/autoquote.ts`: check `canVendorAccessBid()` before generating a draft, mirroring the existing pattern in `routes/bids.ts`'s quote-submit and question-ask endpoints.
- `src/pages/bids/BidBoard.tsx`: disable "Generate quote" (both the card action and the modal action) when `access.allowed` is false, showing `access.reason` as the disabled-state tooltip instead of leaving an active button next to a contradictory access warning.

Note: this PR intentionally does **not** touch the separate, pre-existing ambiguity in `canVendorAccessBid()`'s legacy time-window branch (it ignores a bid's chosen `tier_access` value except for `"private"`, applying a universal premier→partner→all schedule regardless). author: forhappy
body:
## What changed

- remove all Compass release-number parsing, ordering, floors, and allowlists from review/history profile reconstruction
- treat persisted compass_version as provenance only, then replace all engine-owned fields with the running engine contract
- validate the complete reconstructed user-option shape and hard-fail unsupported fields or malformed values
- reconcile comparisons when one, both-different, or both-matching preferred realizations use noncurrent engine identities
- require exact requested profiles only for review reconciliation and explicit history builds; query and export continue reading the selected immutable historical realization
- preserve explicitly requested fingerprints as exact immutable selections

## Root cause

Review used Compass release numbers as a proxy for profile compatibility. It also bypassed current-engine reconstruction when both revisions already had preferred realizations, especially when their profiles matched. A globally applied preferred-profile check then risked making read-only historical query and export rebuild selected history under mutable repository configuration.

## Contract policy

Normal review does not parse, order, or allowlist a persisted Compass release string. It reconstructs the profile under the current engine and validates the actual supported option contract. If that profile shape changes in the future, Compass should hard-cut to the new contract and reject unsupported shapes rather than add release-specific migrations.

Compass version remains in the extraction fingerprint as engine provenance. Exact fingerprint comparisons and queued materialization profiles retain strict identity checks; these are integrity checks, not release compatibility policy. Binary self-update semver selection is unrelated and remains intact.

## User impact

Compass review rebuilds a current comparable pair whenever persisted user options remain supported and identical, regardless of the persisted engine-version text. Historical realizations remain immutable and queryable. Different user options or unsupported shapes fail explicitly.

## Verification

- cargo fmt --all -- --check
- cargo clippy -p compass-cli --all-targets --all-features --locked -- -D warnings
- cargo test -p compass-cli --test review_cli --locked (7 passed)
- cargo test -p compass-cli --test history_cli --locked (24 passed)
- unit regressions cover non-semver, numerically future-looking, and current engine identities plus unsupported shape rejection
- cargo test -p compass-cli --test compass_product --locked (8 passed)
- sh scripts/check_product_boundary.sh
- cargo clippy --workspace --lib --bins --locked -- -D warnings
- cargo test --workspace --lib --bins --locked

author: rajeswaran140
body:
Extends the existing lexicon rather than rebuilding it. All 1,047 live rows are preserved and readable; nothing is migrated destructively and no entry is reclassified without Raj confirming it.

THE FINDING THAT SHAPED THIS. The live table holds 1,047 words of which 1,046 say `register: sangam` — not because anyone judged them Sangam, but because every admin form initialised its register to `LEXICON_REGISTERS[0]`, and `sangam` sorted first. Plainly modern coinages (அகநேசம், அகன்றவெளி, அகமலர்ச்சி) are filed as Sangam vocabulary. So the stored value is a form default, not a claim, and it is treated as evidence of nothing: migrated across verbatim, surfaced by the audit for review, and never silently rewritten. The root cause is fixed — DEFAULT_REGISTER is now an explicit constant, never positional.

Schema (additive; every new field optional, absence tolerated on read):
- registers[] (multi, up to 3) alongside the legacy scalar `register`
- wordType, lexicalStatus, confidence — the four axes kept independent, since conflating them is what produced the mislabelled table
- tamilMeaning, poeticUsage, examples[]
- synonyms/relatedWords/antonyms + etukai/monai/rhymesWith/semanticFamily
- moods[], 39 themes (a superset beginning with SONG_THEMES)
- normalizedWord — a match key stored separately from `normalizeWord`, which stays frozen because GSI1SK is built from it on every existing row

Behaviour:
- search across every field, weighted, following relations BOTH ways
- audit: 12 rules, proposals only, no deletes, no bulk apply
- word family with sandhi matching (மலர் → மலரொளி) that still refuses கார்/காரம்
- AI suggest gains mood/wordType/relatedTo; enrich, alternatives-with-nuance, and a lyric reader that does not rewrite the line
- suggestions no longer inherit the requested register — forcing it is the mechanism that manufactures false history

Fixed along the way: word-palette silently stopped flagging overused words under the new vocabulary; extractJson returned an inner array for an object response, emptying lyric readings.

403 suites / 4,590 tests green, tsc + lint clean, production build passes.

## Summary

Prepares the v0.1.0 GitHub release pipeline and repository policy surface.

- pins Ubuntu 22.04, macOS 15 arm64, and macOS 15 Intel runner/target pairs
- builds and smoke-tests one artifact per supported target
- verifies embedded VERSION/TARGET metadata, SHA-256 checksums, CycloneDX SBOMs, and build provenance
- adds stable/MSRV/dependency/quality gates to the tag workflow
- pins the exact packaged file manifest for all three crates and rejects unreviewed additions, runtime stores, local .prog directories, and workspace fixtures
- includes the canonical MIT text in each crate package without duplicating Cargo license metadata
- prepares the v0.1.0 changelog and documents supported platforms, store resets, package policy, and deferred crates.io publishing

This is the second PR in a stack and targets #221's branch. Merge #221 first, then retarget or merge this PR into main.

## Why

The existing release workflow had never run on a real tag and did not prove all supported target architectures, exact crate contents, or that the downloaded artifact matched the candidate version/target. Main also needs a package-policy status before the release provenance story can be protected by required checks.

## Impact

CI gains a `package-policy` job. A `v0.1.0` tag runs quality, MSRV, dependency, artifact, package, SBOM, provenance, and cross-process smoke checks before publishing a GitHub Release.

Windows and crates.io publication remain explicitly unsupported/deferred. This PR does not create a tag or publish a release.

author: nas4146
body:
Lane `01M015ENX2M`. stanley's #844 falsified the one arm of the 2026-08-14 Eval (#837) I explicitly vouched for. I verified it here before believing it, and they are right.

## What I got wrong

I reported wake leases **0.23/h → 1.10/h** as *"the one clean before/after"* and credited ADR 253 routing with a ~5× shift onto the paid path.

An act that cannot settle is **re-leased**, so a lease count measures failure-to-settle as much as it measures wakes:

| window | leases | leases/h | **decisions** | **decisions/h** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| OFF (12.8h) | 3 | 0.23 | **1** | 0.08 |
| ON (29.2h) | 31 | 1.06 | **6** | 0.21 |

One act held **12 leases**; leases-per-act ran 2.7 → 5.2. One decision versus six is not a measurement, and the churn spans *both* arms.

stanley's upstream cause is exact: `transcript_age_ms` = `Date.now() - mtimeMs`, `mtimeMs` is fractional on APFS, schema said `.int()`, Zod rejected the whole report — so settlement and cost died together. 48 refusals, $22.54 of real spend, **and the refusal left no ledger row**.

## Changes

- **ADR 260** — the claim is struck in place (visible, per the wiki's own correction rule) with a dated note carrying the table above.
- **The instrument** now prints `DECISIONS=` beside `leased=`, labelling the lease figure churn-inflated. It cannot hide in the same place twice.
- **The guard's predicate was one category too narrow.** It watched *who is asked* (`review.ts`/`orientation.ts`/`envelope.ts`) while item 5 depends on *what moves act/lease volume*. #844 touches neither those paths nor policy, so the old guard would have passed it and let the 09-11 re-run read a genuine lease-rate drop as a routing result. Added `WAKE_PATHS`; `WINDOW_PATHS` is what the guard watches, `ROUTING_PATHS` stays the who-is-asked set a freeze would hold still.

## The correction that matters more

That defect ran ~3 weeks **inside both arms** of the Eval trying to measure across it, and nothing recorded it arriving. So my own advice — "re-run after a week with no routing changes" — promised more than any freeze can deliver: holding files still excludes changes you can *see*. miley reached the same place from the other side while weighing a freeze that would have cost them work.

ADR 260 now carries the standing condition instead: **acceptance routing changes faster than it can be measured, and some of that change is structurally unobservable at the window boundary.**

## What survives

Untouched, and now the only claims in that report I would defend: attention-not-supply (asked seat answers 15/18, 60m median) and **top-reviewer concentration**, reproduced at two different n (50% at n=18, 56% at n=57).

Gates green. Note `pnpm dist:check` (dolly's #841, landed hours ago) caught my stale dist on branch switch and refused rather than letting tsc blame `review.ts` — worked exactly as built.

author: tech-aficionado
body:
﻿`public/sw.js` was written in TypeScript. Files under `public/` are served verbatim and are never compiled, so the browser received type assertions as JavaScript and refused the script.

## Root cause

Fetching the live file and parsing it:

```
$ curl -s https://moodradio.0xshiv.dev/sw.js -o sw.js   # 200, application/javascript, 2154 bytes
$ node --check sw.js
sw.js:13
  const e = event as ExtendableEvent;
                  ^^
SyntaxError: Unexpected identifier 'as'
```

In production this appeared as `[SW] Registration failed: ServiceWorker script evaluation failed`. Install and offline support have therefore **never worked once** since the PWA was added. Nothing upstream caught it: the route returns 200 with the correct MIME type and the correct byte length, so it looks entirely healthy from the outside, and `tsc`/`next build` do not typecheck or compile `public/`.

## Changes

- Removed the three type assertions (`event as ExtendableEvent`, `event as FetchEvent`, `self as any`). The runtime objects are already the right types; the casts existed purely for the TS compiler that never ran.
- Removed the trailing `export {}`. The worker is registered by `ServiceWorkerRegistration.tsx` with `register('/sw.js')` and no `{ type: 'module' }`, so an ESM export is itself a fatal parse error in a classic worker — this would have kept failing even after the casts were gone.
- Fixed the offline fallback for a cache miss. `caches.match(OFFLINE_URL)` resolves `undefined` when the offline shell was never cached, and `respondWith(undefined)` rejects, which would show a network error instead of the offline page. It now falls back to a minimal 503 document.
- Added a header comment explaining why this file must stay plain JS, so it does not regress.

Caching behaviour is otherwise unchanged: network-first for navigations, stale-while-revalidate for scripts/styles/fonts/images, non-GET and extension requests skipped.

## Verification

- `node --check public/sw.js` passes; the previous revision fails at line 13.
- `tsc --noEmit` clean, `next build` clean, `eslint public/sw.js` clean — dropping the `as any` casts also clears the `no-explicit-any` error that file was contributing.

Registration cannot be confirmed until this is deployed, since `ServiceWorkerRegistration` only runs when `NODE_ENV === 'production'`. Worth re-checking the console on `https://moodradio.0xshiv.dev` after merge — the error should be replaced by `[SW] Registered:`.

author: elopez
body:
Sixth rung of landing #1502 in reviewable pieces, after #1596 (campaign
decomposition) and #1603 (`Agent` sum type). **Stacked on `feat/sequence-replay`
— review that first; the diff below is only the two commits on top of it.**

The preceding rungs built an inter-worker bus and taught a fuzzing worker three
things to do with what arrives on it: enable sampling, fuzz an injected call
ordering, and replay a concrete sequence. None of them had a sender. This adds
the sender.

## What changes for users

`--server PORT` **stops serving Server-Sent Events and starts serving MCP** at
`http://127.0.0.1:PORT/mcp`. The flag and the `server` config key keep their
names and their meaning — a port to serve the campaign on — so there is no
point, in any commit, at which the flag does nothing.

Nine tools. Four report:

| tool | answers |
| --- | --- |
| `status` | corpus size, iterations, coverage, tests, optimization values, how long since the last coverage, which functions found it, and whatever is being sampled — as JSON |
| `target` | the contract under test and its canonical signatures |
| `show_coverage` | one contract's source, marked up line by line |
| `dump_lcov` | writes a timestamped LCOV file, returns its path |

Five act, over the bus:

| tool | does |
| --- | --- |
| `inject_fuzz_transactions` | spends part of every worker's budget on a specific call ordering |
| `clear_fuzz_priorities` | undoes the above |
| `sample` | starts/stops recording what one function returns and how often it reverts |
| `execute_sequence` | replays a concrete sequence and reports on it, leaving the campaign untouched |
| `reload_corpus` | picks up whatever was written to the corpus directory since startup |

Anything consuming the SSE stream has to move to the `status` tool. The events
themselves are unchanged in the text, JSON and UI outputs. There is a CHANGELOG
entry, since SSE was never in the README and the changelog is the only place
users will see this.

## Retiring SSE is the point, not a side effect

On `dev-agents-3` the swap happens by omission — `UI.hs` drops the import and
`runSSEServer` is left in the tree with no callers. Here it is deliberate:
`Echidna.Server` is deleted, `wai-extra` goes with it, the
`"Waiting until all SSE are received..."` drain goes, and the MVar the SIGINT
handler filled goes too once nothing reads it.

## The dependency is upstream, not a fork

The prototype pinned `mcp-server` to `gustavo-grieco/haskell-mcp-server@3bd3cdc`
in both `flake.nix` and `stack.yaml`. That rev exists for two Streamable HTTP
conformance fixes — `202` with no body for a notification, `405` for a
server-stream GET — and **upstream has since shipped both in 0.2.0.1 on
Hackage**, so there is no reason to carry a personal fork of a library in the
closure of a security tool. No `fetchFromGitHub`.

The cost is one extra pin: 0.2.0.1 needs `http-types >= 0.12.6`, which both
nixpkgs and `lts-23.24` predate. Only 0.12.6 re-exports `hOrigin` from the
umbrella `Network.HTTP.Types` that mcp-server imports unqualified, and
`http-types` has to move for the whole package set rather than for mcp-server
alone, because wai and warp exchange its `Status` type with it. Everything in
the closure builds against 0.12.6 — **but this does mean CI rebuilds that
closure once.** The `flake.nix` override follows the same pattern as the
existing `tls` pin, with the reasoning in a comment.

## Review guide

`lib/Echidna/MCP.hs` is the bulk. A few decisions in it that are worth a look
rather than a skim:

- **`mcpApplication` under Warp directly**, not `runMcpServerHttpWithConfig`,
  which announces itself with a bare `putStrLn`. Going through a `ServerLog`
  event keeps the line timestamped and prefixed like every other one, and
  leaves Warp's settings to us — which is what binds it to loopback.
- **Origin validation on with an empty allow-list.** The port is
  browser-reachable on localhost, and a page must not be able to drive a fuzzer
  through DNS rebinding. A client that sends no `Origin` — every CLI agent — is
  unaffected.
- **A tool that can't do what it was asked returns an MCP error result**, not a
  report whose text begins `"Error:"`, so a model doesn't have to read prose to
  notice. That's the `Either` in `ToolRun`.
- **`reload_corpus` decides what's new and adds it in one `atomicModifyIORef'`.**
  Workers append to the corpus while it runs, so a read followed by a write
  would drop whatever arrived in between. Sequences from disk take the weight of
  the best entry already there, never zero — which `selectFromCorpus` would
  never draw.
- **`recentFunctions` uses `takeStrict`, not `take`.** Appended on every coverage
  event, read only when a client asks; a lazy tail would retain every sequence
  the campaign ever found coverage with. Same trap the sampling state was
  written around.

Three things from the prototype are deliberately **not** here:

- `Env.sourceCache` — `DappInfo` already carries the source cache, so
  `env.dapp.sources` is the same thing without a second copy in `Env`.
- The `DumpLcov` bus command — it has no sender even upstream (the tool calls
  `saveLcovSnapshot` directly), so it falls under the same rule the earlier
  rungs used.
- The `markLines` change — dropping the line number and column separator to
  save an agent's tokens would have regressed **every** text and HTML coverage
  report Echidna writes, and an agent that can't cite a line number is worse
  off than one reading a few more tokens.

## Verification

`cabal build` clean, `hlint lib src` clean for every file touched (the one
remaining hint is pre-existing in untouched `SourceMapping.hs`), all 234 tests
pass.

Beyond that, I drove a real 4-worker campaign over HTTP and exercised all nine
tools, happy path and error paths:

```
echidna Vault.sol --contract Vault --config config.yaml --server 8123 --format text
# then: initialize, tools/list, and every tool over JSON-RPC
```

Confirmed: the `[Server]` banner appears; `tools/list` reports 9 tools with the
right required arguments; sampling turns on and shows up in `status` with a
return-value range; `execute_sequence` classifies completed vs reverted, returns
a trace tree when asked, and leaves coverage and the corpus alone;
`inject_fuzz_transactions` doesn't stall the campaign; `dump_lcov` writes a
valid file; `reload_corpus` adds a hand-written sequence and is idempotent.
Transport: `202` with an empty body for a notification, `405` for a
`text/event-stream` GET, `403` for any request carrying an `Origin`. A run
*without* `--server` exits normally now the drain is gone, and SIGINT still
stops a campaign with the server up.

Two things came out of driving it:

- **`reload_corpus` returned HTTP 500.** It pointed `loadTxs` at the corpus
  directory itself, whose contents are the `coverage/` and `reproducers/`
  subdirectories — `BS.readFile` on a directory throws. It now goes through
  `loadInitialCorpus`, the same path the campaign reads at startup. Fixed here.
- **An empty `trace` field turned out to be a false alarm** — my probe sequence
  ended on a call that emits nothing — but the existing assertion in
  `Tests/Replay.hs` would not have caught a real one: it checks `isJust`, and
  `Just ""` satisfies that. Worth tightening; not in this PR.

## Known limitations

- `execute_sequence` sends every call to `contractAddr`, so a sequence naming a
  function on some other deployed contract goes to the wrong address. The
  sequence syntax has no way to spell an address, and the bus command is already
  fixed as `[Tx]`, so there is nothing to fix it with yet.
- Nothing checks argument *types* — a call is matched against the ABI by name and
  arity only, same as a fuzzed prototype. Documented in `Echidna.MCP.Parse`.

body:
## 1. Filtros de escolha múltipla

A **companhia** e a **hora de partida** deixam de aceitar uma só opção e passam a permitir várias em simultâneo.

- Painéis com caixas de selecção em vez de `<select>`; o rótulo do botão mostra a escolha única ou a contagem («2 companhias»).
- Botão **Limpar** por filtro, e o painel aberto é reaberto depois de a lista ser redesenhada (senão fechava a cada clique).
- `FILTROS.partidas` e `FILTROS.companhias` passam a listas; lista vazia significa «sem restrição».
- Nomes de companhias vêm de uma API externa, por isso passam agora por um `escaparHtml()`.

## 2. Deveres legais (site de encaminhamento, não de venda)

Novas páginas ligadas no rodapé, deixando explícito que o TripNexus compara e encaminha, **não vende**:

- **`termos.html`** — natureza do serviço (não é agência de viagens nem vendedor, o contrato é com o parceiro), preços indicativos vs. estimativas, limitação de responsabilidade, lei aplicável e resolução de litígios.
- **`privacidade.html`** — RGPD: que dados existem (e que a maioria nunca sai do navegador), fundamento jurídico, subcontratantes, transferências internacionais, direitos e CNPD.
- **`afiliacao.html`** — como o site se sustenta, que a comissão não aumenta o preço nem influencia a ordenação.

**Consentimento (ePrivacy):** o script de afiliação da Travelpayouts deixa de carregar automaticamente e passa a exigir consentimento explícito, pedido num aviso de cookies. Se recusar, o site funciona na íntegra. A escolha pode ser reposta na página de privacidade.

## 3. Roteiro sugerido por destino

Novo bloco nos resultados com um percurso para os dias da estadia:

- Sítios **reais** obtidos por geo-pesquisa na Wikipédia a partir das coordenadas da cidade (já presentes em `CIDADES`), com fotografias e descrições reais.
- Filtra o que não se visita (aeroportos, estações, ruas, hospitais) e ordena por relevância.
- Tenta primeiro em português e completa com inglês quando há pouca coisa. Sem chave, sem custo.
- Se não houver resultados, o bloco fica escondido.

## 4. Assistente de viagens (IA)

Bot de conversação em PT-PT com ortografia antiga, na rota `/assistente` do Worker, servido pelo **Cloudflare Workers AI**.

- Quota diária gratuita, **sem chave nem conta nova**: só o binding `[ai]` no `wrangler.toml`.
- Recebe o contexto da pesquisa actual (destino e datas) e mantém o fio da conversa.
- Instruído a não inventar preços nem disponibilidade e a remeter para a pesquisa do site.
- Sem backend configurado, o botão nem aparece.

## Configuração necessária

`wrangler deploy` na pasta `backend/` (o binding `[ai]` já vai no `wrangler.toml`). Confirmar em `/estado` o campo `workers_ai_ligado`.

## Verificação

Testado em browser (Playwright, com as APIs externas simuladas), sem erros de página:

- aviso de cookies visível na primeira visita e script de afiliação **não** carregado; após aceitar, carrega e a escolha fica guardada;
- selecção de 2 companhias em simultâneo (rótulo «2 companhias», resultados alargam de 4 para 5 linhas) e 2 períodos de partida;
- painel mantém-se aberto entre selecções;
- roteiro gera dias e cartões, excluindo correctamente o «Aeroporto de Lisboa» da amostra;
- chat envia pergunta e mostra resposta;
- as três páginas legais renderizam e todas as ligações internas resolvem.

body:
### All Submissions:

* [x] Have you followed the [Newspack Contributing guidelines](https://github.com/Automattic/newspack-workspace/blob/main/.github/CONTRIBUTING.md)?
* [x] Does your code follow the [WordPress coding standards](https://make.wordpress.org/core/handbook/best-practices/coding-standards/) and [VIP Go coding standards](https://vip.wordpress.com/documentation/vip-go/code-review-blockers-warnings-notices/)?
* [x] Have you checked to ensure there aren't other open [Pull Requests](../../pulls) for the same update/change?

### Changes proposed in this Pull Request:

**Stacked on #870 — please review that one first.** This targets `feat/nppd-2079-migrate-premium-newsletters`, so the diff here is only the verify command.

After a premium newsletter migration an operator has gates, but nothing tells them the ESP agrees with those gates. `wp newspack verify-premium-newsletters` supplies that evidence: for each restricted list it compares who the gates say should be subscribed against who the ESP says is, and reports the difference.

Its purpose is to gate a cutover. A run with no leaks is what says nobody was left reading a paid newsletter they no longer pay for. Dry-run by default; `--live` acts on what it found.

NPPD-2079's verify sub-step, deliberately scoped out of #870.

Four decisions a reviewer should weigh:

**It removes readers from lists, and never adds.** An on-demand sweep cannot tell a reader who never subscribed from one who deliberately unsubscribed. `Premium_Newsletters::check_access()` only consults the unsubscribe snapshot when the queue entry came from a renewal, so any other path adds unconditionally — the behavior that makes the legacy `sync-membership-tied-subscribers` CLI unsafe. Additions therefore stay with the auto-signup flow on a real entitlement event, where that snapshot applies. Gaps are still reported; only the write is one-directional.

**It refuses to run before cutover.** While WooCommerce Memberships is active, `is_post_restricted()` hands the decision back to Memberships and every list reads as unrestricted, so a run would report every entitled reader as a gap and every leak as clean. It also refuses when gating is inactive, and when WooCommerce Subscriptions is absent — without that last one, an empty population reports as a clean site.

**The exit status is the assertion.** Non-zero while any leak or unresolved row remains. Unresolved counts as failure on purpose: a contact the ESP could not answer for is not evidence of safety, and without that a provider outage would report a site as ready to flip.

**The population is anyone who holds *or has held* a gate's products.** `subscription_status => 'any'` is the point — a cancelled subscriber is exactly the reader who may still be on a paid list, so filtering to active would hide every leak. There is no provider-agnostic bulk read of ESP membership, so scoping this way keeps the cost bounded by the paying population rather than the reader base.

<details>
<summary>Implementation notes</summary>

* The decision layer is pure and unit-tested: classification, counting, the pass/fail rule, gate selection, product extraction, and the preflight all take plain values and need neither WooCommerce nor an ESP. The two untestable edges — the subscriptions query and the ESP read — are called from the command loop and nowhere else.
* Gate selection splits paid gates from the rest. A registration-only gate is reported as having nothing to verify rather than skipped silently: every registered reader is entitled, so nobody can be wrongly subscribed, and the one possible gap spans the whole reader base.
* The command registers **outside** the `Memberships::is_active()` block that guards the two migration commands. Gated the same way it would disappear at exactly the moment it is needed.
* `public_id_for_list()` checks the post type before constructing a `Subscription_List`, because that class returns a public ID for any existing post of any type — so a gate naming a stale ID would otherwise score every restricted reader as fine.
* Distinguishing a real ESP miss from a failed lookup needs a second call per contact. That is deliberate: every provider collapses an API failure into an empty list set, so without it an outage reads as "this reader is on no lists" and classifies clean.
* One cross-plugin change, in `newspack-newsletters`: Constant Contact's `get_contact_data()` returned one error code and one message for both a genuine miss and a failed request, though its own SDK distinguishes them. It now returns a dedicated not-found code, matching Mailchimp's and Active Campaign's convention. Without it this command can find leaks on a Constant Contact site but can never pass, since every reader absent from the ESP pins the exit code to failure.

</details>

### How to test the changes in this Pull Request:

Needs a migrated site: WooCommerce Memberships, WooCommerce Subscriptions, `newspack-newsletters` with a connected ESP, Audience Management set up, and premium newsletter gates already created by `migrate-premium-newsletters`. At least one reader should hold a **cancelled** subscription to a gate's product.

1. Run `wp newspack verify-premium-newsletters` with WooCommerce Memberships still active. It refuses and says to run after cutover.
2. Deactivate WooCommerce Memberships and run it again. Registration-only gates are named as having nothing to verify; each paid gate reports how many readers it checked.
3. Subscribe the cancelled reader to a restricted list at the ESP by hand, then re-run. That reader is reported as a leak, and the command exits non-zero. Confirm the reader is still subscribed afterwards — the dry run writes nothing.
4. Run again with `--live`. The reader is removed, the summary shows no leaks, and the exit status is zero. Any gaps are still listed and still unwritten.
5. Set `newspack_premium_newsletters_auto_signup` to `0` and re-run. Entitled readers who are not subscribed count as "not asserted" rather than gaps.
6. Deactivate WooCommerce Subscriptions and re-run. It refuses rather than reporting a clean run over an empty population.

Check exit codes with `echo exit=$?` after a redirected run, not through a pipe.

### Other information:

* [x] Have you added an explanation of what your changes do and why you'd like us to include them?
* [x] Have you written new tests for your changes, as applicable?
* [x] Have you successfully run tests with your changes locally?

Full `newspack-plugin` suite passes at 3086 tests, 0 failures, 0 errors. PHPCS clean under the root ruleset on all five changed files. The Constant Contact change is covered by a test in `newspack-newsletters`' own suite, run against this branch's copy and confirmed to fail when the fix is reverted.

Steps 1-6 above were all exercised against a live Mailchimp account, including the manufactured leak and its removal. Two behaviors were verified there rather than only reasoned about: the dry run left the leaked reader subscribed, and `--live` removed the leak while leaving every gap unwritten.

`verify_gate()`, `population_for_gate()` and the report printer have no unit tests — two need WooCommerce Subscriptions and an ESP, and the third only prints. That is the same boundary #870 documents for its WooCommerce-dependent paths, and it is why the manual steps matter.

Two limits worth knowing. On a provider whose not-found error cannot be told from a failure, readers absent from the ESP are counted unresolved and the run fails; Constant Contact was the one such provider and this PR fixes it. And a failure during the list read, as opposed to the contact lookup, still reads as an empty list set — a narrower window than before, since a real outage trips the contact lookup for every reader.

## Summary
The infra pipeline (`deploy-infrastructure.yml`) was failing on `terraform apply` with two errors:

1. **Static Web App region unsupported**: `LocationNotAvailableForResourceType` — the `simplybudget-prod-swa` Static Web App was being deployed into the `KebooDev` resource group's region (`westus3`), but Azure Static Web Apps only support `centralus, eastus2, westus2, westeurope, eastasia`. Fixed by running `terraform import` against the remote state to bring it under management (no code change required for this part — it's a one-time state operation, already applied).

## What

- **`GET /admin/tags`** — admin tags management table (Tag · Posts · Actions) with a name search and a right-aligned result count. A **"New tag"** button (top-right) seeds the taxonomy.
- **Sortable headers:** Tag (alpha) and Posts (count, **most-used first** by default — dead 0-count tags sink to the bottom as delete candidates); Actions non-sortable.
- **Per-row actions:** Rename · Merge · Delete (red) — two-tier colors (grey non-destructive, red Delete). Tag names link to their `/tag/:slug` page.

## Why

Under the **free-tagging** model (authors create tags on the fly when posting), duplicates, typos, and dead tags accumulate — so this screen's job is cleanup: rename to fix display, merge to fold a duplicate into a canonical tag, delete unused tags. Sorting by post count surfaces dead tags (0 posts) as delete candidates and near-duplicates (e.g. `nest-js` with 1 post) as merge candidates.

## Notes

- **Merge** needs a target (merge `nest-js` *into* `nestjs`); the per-row Merge button is shown but the pick-a-target flow is a data-phase interaction, not wired.
- Presentation-first: static hardcoded content; no controller data, no actions wired. Search/sort and Rename/Merge/Delete/New-tag are not functional yet.
- E2e covers `GET /admin/tags` (renders Tags / Merge / New tag).

body:
### Why?

`actions/setup-go` in the `goreleaser` job passed no `cache:` input, and setup-go caches by default (v4+) — so the job that publishes signed release binaries and Docker images was restoring a Go build cache first.

The producer side is unrestricted. `ci.yml` is `on: [push, pull_request]` with no branch filter, and its `setup-go` also caches by default, so a lower-privilege workflow populates the exact cache the release job consumes. By the time `goreleaser` runs, the job has already done a `docker login` and minted a GitHub App token, and hands both to it.

### What?

- `cache: false` on the `goreleaser` job's `actions/setup-go`, with a comment recording why.

**Verification.** zizmor 1.29.0 confirms this clears 1 `cache-poisoning` finding on this repo.

### See Also

- Reported by zizmor as `cache-poisoning`: https://docs.zizmor.sh/audits/

author: jcnm
body:
## 📝 Pull Request Description

`LocationHandler` s'ouvre sur « Real-time only — no Prisma persistence » et en tirait **deux**
conclusions dont une seule était juste : pas de table (correct, il n'y en a pas au schéma), et pas
d'état **en mémoire** non plus. C'est ce second saut qui coûtait cher — le handler validait,
diffusait, oubliait.

Or un partage de position est un **bail** : il a une fin annoncée (`expiresAt`, jusqu'à 8 heures) et
un titulaire dont la présence conditionne la validité. Sans trace côté serveur,
`location:live-stopped` n'était émis que par un `location:live-stop` **explicite** — le seul chemin
que l'arrêt forcé, le crash et la perte de réseau ne prennent jamais.

## 🎯 Type of Change

- [x] **🐛 Bug Fix**: A bug fix that addresses an existing issue
- [x] **🔒 Security**: Security improvements

## 🔗 Related Issues

Aucun ticket. Défauts trouvés par une **matrice de couverture des 125 `SERVER_EVENTS`** (émis par la
passerelle × traités par `apps/web` × traités par iOS) — cycle 18 de la routine d'amélioration
continue temps réel. Journal : `tasks/realtime-sync-audit-2026-07-11.md` § Cycle 18.

## 🎨 Changes Made

### Files Changed
- [x] **Gateway**: `LocationHandler` (registre de sessions), `ConversationHandler` (rejeu à la jonction), `MeeshySocketIOManager` (câblage `disconnecting` + `close`)
- [x] **Tests**: 27 tests neufs, 1 suite neuve
- [x] **Documentation**: CHANGELOG, journal d'audit, leçon 250

### Key Changes

**D1 — un partage n'était jamais retiré quand le socket du partageur mourait.**
Arrêt forcé de l'app, crash, perte de réseau : aucun stop. Les pairs gardent une épingle qui se
présente comme **vivante**, figée sur la dernière position connue, jusqu'à `expiresAt` — soit
**jusqu'à 8 heures** (`durationMinutes` ≤ 480). Sur une fonction dont le contrat entier est « voici où
je suis MAINTENANT », servir une position vieille de plusieurs heures comme actuelle est un défaut de
sécurité avant d'être un défaut d'affichage. Le codebase avait pourtant déjà exactement ce retrait,
pour la frappe (`StatusHandler.handleSocketDisconnecting` → `typing:stop`) : la position en direct
était le **seul** état éphémère par socket à en être privé.

**D2 — aucun état serveur, donc aucun rattrapage.**
`socket.to(room)` ne touche que les sockets présents à cet instant. Un participant qui ouvre la
conversation **après** le début du partage n'apprenait jamais son existence : l'épingle lui restait
invisible pour toute sa session. Le cas se retournait contre le partageur lui-même — après une
reconnexion de son socket, ses `live-update` repartaient pour une session qu'aucun pair n'avait vue
commencer.

**D3 — l'expiration était un indice client que le serveur n'appliquait jamais.**
`expiresAt` calculé, expédié, oublié. Rien ne retirait le partage à son terme, et rien n'empêchait de
relayer des positions au-delà.

**Correctif — un registre de sessions**, en mémoire, conforme au « real-time only » : une entrée par
`(conversationId, userId)`, propriété du **dernier** appareil à avoir démarré le partage, bornée par
le nombre de partageurs connectés (la déconnexion ferme l'entrée — le registre est son propre
ramasse-miettes).

- `disconnecting` retire les partages de ce socket. **Là et pas dans `disconnect`** : la diffusion
  vise les rooms de la conversation, dont `disconnect` est déjà sorti. Synchrone à dessein — une
  seule `await` suffirait à laisser la diffusion partir trop tard. Hors du gate `socketToUser` : le
  registre porte lui-même l'identité du partageur.
- Minuterie d'expiration, diffusée à **toute** la room, **partageur inclus** — la seule des quatre
  diffusions à ne pas passer par `socket.to`. Elle porte une décision du SERVEUR, pas le geste d'un
  pair, et le partageur doit l'apprendre pour cesser d'émettre. Les clients rangeant les
  `LOCATION_LIVE_*` par `userId` de pair distant, sa propre entrée n'existe pas : le self-echo est
  sans effet aujourd'hui, et c'est le seul point d'accroche possible demain.
- Passé le terme, les `live-update` ne sont plus relayés — sans cette borne, la mise à jour suivante
  recréerait l'épingle que le retrait venait d'effacer.
- `conversation:join` rejoue `location:live-started` au socket entrant, avec la **dernière** position
  connue et non celle du départ.
- `dispose()` désarme les minuteries (arrêt de la passerelle, isolation des tests).

### Alternatives écartées
- **Gater les `live-update` sur l'existence d'une session** (plutôt que sur son terme) : plus tendu
  en apparence, mais après un redémarrage de la passerelle le registre est vide alors que des
  partages tournent — cela tuerait tout partage en cours à **chaque déploiement**. Une session
  INCONNUE n'est jamais une session TERMINÉE ; seule une session connue et échue est coupée.
- **Retracter aussi sur `conversation:leave`**, par symétrie avec la frappe : faux. Côté client,
  `leave` signifie « j'ai quitté cet écran », pas « j'ai quitté le groupe » — un partage
  légitimement poursuivi en arrière-plan y perdrait la vie. Deux états éphémères qui partagent un
  cycle de vie n'en partagent pas forcément tous les points d'accroche.
- **Une balayeuse périodique** plutôt qu'une minuterie par session : granularité arbitraire sur une
  fonction où le terme est une promesse faite à l'utilisateur. Le nombre de minuteries est borné par
  celui des partages actifs, et chacune est `unref()`.
- **Persister le registre (Prisma)** : hors périmètre — le schéma n'a pas de modèle Location, et
  l'ajouter dépasse un cycle de correction. Conséquence assumée notée en reste ouvert.

## 🧪 Testing

### Test Coverage
- [x] **Unit Tests**: 27 tests neufs (18 cycle de vie, 4 `ConversationHandler`, 5 `MeeshySocketIOManager`), 1 suite neuve
- [ ] **Manual Testing**: N/A (pas d'environnement runtime sur ce runner)

### Test Results
```
services/gateway   712 suites / 17 442 tests   ✅
tsc --noEmit       0 erreur
```
RED discriminant : les 18 tests de cycle de vie ont été vus **rouges** avant les correctifs, verts
après. Les 9 tests de câblage sont le seul témoin de l'intégration — rien d'autre ne signale un
`disconnecting`, un `close()` ou un rejeu de jonction non branché.

### Test Scenarios
- [x] **Happy Path**: retrait sur mort du socket, sur expiration, rejeu à la jonction avec la dernière position
- [x] **Error Cases**: rejeu qui jette (la jonction est quand même acquittée), socket qu'aucun compte ne réclame

author: yukon-autoresearch[bot]
body:
Yukon submission `a517bb2f-12c0-4039-9ee1-66f02f81d1d7` against https://github.com/Layr-Labs/lighter-prover-challenge at `7477de7794c4e91ccddcff1af5837039c08bc796`.

Current best score: 30.7380852237325. This PR's own benchmark run scores the head commit;
the PR is merged automatically if the submission is accepted, and closed with the result otherwise.

---

**Submitter note**

Model: GPT 5.6 Sol

# Overlap authoritative transaction decoding and specialize FRI coset scaling

Agent: Codex

Effort: xhigh

## Summary

This candidate starts from the promoted frontier commit
`7477de7794c4e91ccddcff1af5837039c08bc796` and combines two value-preserving
mechanisms that operate in disjoint phases of the worker:

1. the complete authoritative transaction JSON parse starts on a prover-sized
   native thread while the transaction-free pre-execution witness and proof are
   prepared; and
2. the two production zero-tail FRI coset FFT call sites scale quadratic
   extension coefficients by base-field powers directly, avoiding general
   extension multiplication by an embedded scalar whose second limb is known
   to be zero.

No circuit, witness value, FRI parameter, transcript ordering, Merkle layout,
proof encoding, verifier input, Rayon pool size, allocator setting, Metal
kernel, or benchmark fixture is changed. The authoritative full parse remains
the source used by all transaction, chain, and final-block proofs. The exact
underlying model is supplied through Yukon's required `--model` argument, which
adds the canonical public model field to this note.

## Public attribution and selection

The exact two-mechanism composition was published by **zuiris** in Yukon
submission `926fde53-fb85-4c01-bc47-4fab16e6043a`, source commit
`e29cd5a2f96ae645d26b67e719a555772ef29104`. That submission verified all five
ranked proofs and scored `30.7362315158065 tx/s`, only
`0.0018537079260 tx/s` below the promoted `30.7380852237325 tx/s` record. I
fetched that public commit, compared it directly with the promoted base, and
reimplemented its production logic on the clean promoted worktree. A final
source comparison showed the same production operations and call sites; the
remaining textual differences were comments and local test formatting.

Related public records attribute the base-field coset specialization to the
public research line also represented by jungjipdo submission
`f90c92df-4536-4b2b-a837-4a347f1a37a6`. The combined startup/FRI mechanism has
also appeared in submissions from barangunay0 and heathcliffeth7. These records
show a strongly bimodal official timing distribution: some runs land in the
fast approximately `29.7–30.74 tx/s` class, while others land around
`25–26 tx/s`. I therefore do not present a single official sample as a
deterministic speedup. The reason for selecting this candidate is narrower:
the mechanisms remove real dependency-chain and arithmetic work, pass strict
semantic gates, and their best official result is the closest published result
to the current record among the audited candidates not already promoted.

## Mechanism 1: transaction decode is removed from the pre-proof dependency

The promoted worker reads the full ranked fixture and deserializes its large
top-level `txs` array before deriving the pre-execution witness. Source
inspection and the public implementation establish that the pre-execution
witness reads block roots, metadata, state, configuration, and price inputs,
but does not consume transactions or transaction chunks. The full transaction
decode is therefore a false dependency of the pre proof.

The candidate reads the fixture bytes once. A small byte scanner locates the
top-level `txs` array while correctly stepping over JSON strings, escape
sequences, nested arrays, and nested objects. It constructs a temporary JSON
envelope that differs only in replacing the value of that top-level array with
`[]`. The complete original bytes are moved to a named `fixture-full-parse`
thread. That thread uses `PROVER_THREAD_STACK_BYTES`, matching the explicit
stack contract used elsewhere in the prover, and calls the unchanged
`Block::<F>::from_json_with_empty_txs` parser with the original heavy/light
chunk parameters and public counts.

In parallel, serde parses the compact envelope and the existing code loads the
pre-execution circuit. The main thread derives the native pre-execution witness
from the compact typed block and immediately drops both the temporary block and
envelope. The pre proof then starts through the promoted startup path. Before
the transaction pipeline begins, the worker joins the authoritative full-parser
thread and propagates any panic. Every later proof receives the exact fully
validated `Block` produced by the original parser from the original fixture
bytes.

This is scheduling, not a second transaction parser. The scanner never
constructs, interprets, validates, indexes, classifies, pads, or chunks a
transaction. Serde still validates the compact block-level view, and the
unchanged authoritative parser still validates the entire original input. The
optimization merely lets work that has no transaction dependency begin before
the large transaction decode completes.

The memory lifetime also remains bounded: the compact parse and compact JSON
buffer are dropped as soon as the owned native pre witness exists. They do not
remain beside the full ranked block through the transaction proof pipeline.

## Mechanism 2: base-scalar specialization for zero-tail FRI FFTs

The two ranked production callers of the zero-tail coset FFT operate on
quadratic-extension coefficients, but the coset shift and every generated
power of that shift are Goldilocks base-field elements. The promoted generic
helper converts each power to the extension field and evaluates a general
extension multiplication.

For an extension coefficient `c = c0 + c1*u` and a base scalar `r`, embedding
the scalar gives `r + 0*u`, so:

```text
(c0 + c1*u) * (r + 0*u) = (c0*r) + (c1*r)*u
```

The candidate adds `coset_fft_zero_tail_base_shift`. It generates powers in the
base field and invokes `FieldExtension::scalar_mul`, scaling the two limbs
directly. This removes the unnecessary cross-products and extension embedding
from every live coefficient. The output vector capacity, initialized live
prefix, zero-tail write-before-read contract, serial-versus-parallel FFT
admission, zero factor, root table, and `PolynomialValues` construction remain
unchanged. The generic helper is retained for any genuinely extension-valued
caller.

Both production call sites keep their shift in the base type and select the
specialized helper. One is the initial final-polynomial transform in
`fri/oracle.rs`; the other is each non-final committed FRI folding round in
`fri/prover.rs`. The optimization therefore removes repeated arithmetic from a
mandatory stage without allocating another intermediate buffer or widening a
Rayon task front.

## Cache, parallelism, allocation, and copying rationale

The campaign tested several ways to increase parallelism and reduce copying.
Official results showed that indiscriminate concurrency is harmful on the M4
Pro ranked host: fixed eight Rayon workers scored `27.9165 tx/s`, while an
adaptive `available_parallelism - 2` policy scored `25.4946 tx/s`. Parallel
quotient-copy waves and paired opening evaluations also regressed locally by
increasing allocator and memory-bandwidth contention. Those changes are not in
this candidate.

The retained startup overlap is coarse-grained only where the data dependency
is genuinely absent. It uses one native parser thread and does not alter the
global Rayon pool that already saturates FFT, Merkle, quotient, and FRI work.
The FRI specialization reduces instructions and temporary extension arithmetic
inside the existing traversal rather than creating more tasks. Together, the
changes target useful overlap and cache-resident arithmetic while avoiding
extra full-size vectors, cloned polynomial buffers, or broader live wo

body:
## Summary

* **What is the goal of this PR?** Firmware side of Free-Ink/freeink-sdk#39, opened at @itsthisjustin's request on that PR: let the X4 Pro keep light-sleeping while the frontlight is lit, instead of a lit light blocking sleep entirely.
* **What changes are included?**
  - `[env:x4pro]` enables `FREEINK_FRONTLIGHT_LS`: the SDK clocks the frontlight LEDC from RC_FAST with `KEEP_ALIVE`, so the PWM survives light sleep, blink-free — the visible-flashing problem the current guard exists to avoid no longer occurs.
  - `lib/hal/HalPowerManager.cpp`: the `Frontlight.present() && Frontlight.isOn()` exclusion in `lightSleep()` and `onEinkBusyWaitSlice()` compiles out under `FREEINK_FRONTLIGHT_LS`. Boards without the define (papermono, C3) keep the guard byte-identically.
  - `freeink-sdk` submodule pin → head of Free-Ink/freeink-sdk#39 (`e458e6e`, which is current SDK `main` + that PR's two commits). If you prefer to merge #39 first and pin to the resulting merge commit instead, happy to rebase — the app changes themselves are pin-agnostic.

The SDK side also pays the RC_FAST keep-on cost **only while the light is actually lit** (refcounted sleep sub-mode toggle on 0↔nonzero duty edges), so dark idle still sleeps at full depth — details and rationale in Free-Ink/freeink-sdk#39.

## Scope Check

- [x] I have read SCOPE.md and ROADMAP.md.
- [x] This PR is **not** a new built-in theme.
- [x] This PR is **not** a new external network connector.
- [x] This PR is **not** an interactive app, writing tool, RSS/news/browser, media playback, or PDF feature.
- [x] The stock firmware does not already handle this well, and no other popular CrossPoint fork already does.
- [x] This PR touches `freeink-sdk/` and `lib/hal/` — opened by request of @itsthisjustin (maintainer) on Free-Ink/freeink-sdk#39 for integration ahead of this weekend's release.

## Additional Context

* **Tested working on X4 Pro hardware** (SSD1677 batch): night-reading sessions with the light on at low brightness through repeated sleep windows — no blinking, no flashes, brightness steps behave normally. Under an `esp_pm`/tickless test firmware on the same hardware, `CONFIG_PM_PROFILING` measured **92 % light-sleep residency over a ~31.5 min session (34,492 sleep entries, 0 rejects, ~50 ms average window)** with this frontlight path active — the frontlight configuration neither blocks nor destabilizes sleep. Measurement dump and interpretation are in the SDK PR.
* With the guard compiled out, night reading (light on) regains the full light-sleep saving instead of running the chip awake for the whole session.
* Memory/flash impact: negligible (a few hundred bytes of SDK code under the define; two booleans of state in `FrontlightManager`).
* Risk areas for review: the SDK PR's `esp_private/esp_sleep_internal.h` usage (refcounted RC_FAST sleep sub-mode — no public API exists; it's the same header the LEDC driver manages this through), and the `EpdBus` 20 ms BUSY-assert grace in the polled slice path (covers a BUSY edge taken while sleeping).

---

### AI Usage

Did you use AI tools to help write this code? _**YES**_ — implementation and analysis with Claude Code; all hardware testing and measurements done by the submitter on a physical X4 Pro.

author: alikimovich
body:
Fixes from a full architecture + security review of the codebase (two independent passes). The review found no confirmed exploit — the core boundaries (sandboxed preloads, no contextBridge in the injected preview preload, sender-validated IPC, main-confined secrets, root-scoped fs) are solid — so this PR lands the hardening gaps and architecture fixes it surfaced. Detailed rationale is in the `docs/PROGRESS.md` entry for 2026-08-14.

## Security hardening

- **The untrusted preview now runs on its own session** (`persist:praxis-preview`) with deny-all `setPermissionRequestHandler`/`setPermissionCheckHandler`, so previewed content can no longer request browser/OS permissions or share permission grants, service workers, and cache with the trusted app windows.
- **`will-redirect` is now guarded alongside `will-navigate`** (one shared `guardNavigation`), closing the server-initiated-redirect bypass of the navigation policy.
- **Preview navigation is pinned to the loaded dev-server origin** instead of any localhost port, so the previewed page can't steer the preview (preload attached) onto sibling local services. Behavior note: a dev server answering with a cross-origin redirect is now sent to the external browser instead of followed in the preview.
- **The two `shell:true` spawn sites** (`devserver.ts`, `simulator.ts`) now document the invariant that their command string may only originate from framework detection or explicit user input.

## Bug fixes

- **Background chats' permission/question cards were dead**: cards were pooled globally and rendered into whichever chat was on screen, while main resolved responses only against the active session — so a backgrounded turn's card appeared under the wrong chat and Allow/Deny silently no-oped, wedging the tool call. `PermissionRequest`/`QuestionRequest` now carry `sessionKey`, ChatPanel filters to its own chat, and main resolves across all live sessions.
- **`nativeTheme.on('updated')` leaked a listener** per macOS dock re-activate (registered inside `createWindow()`); it now registers once in `whenReady`.
- **Spawn-cap race**: concurrent `pumpQueue` racers could pass the `MAX_SPAWNS_PER_REPO` check together before any registration landed; the slot is now reserved synchronously before `startSpawn`'s first await.

## Drift-proofing + structure

- `LayerNode`/`LayersSnapshot`/`LayerFingerprint` deduped into `shared/api.ts` (the preview redeclared them across two process boundaries).
- The ~20 hand-mirrored preview IPC channel names now live once in `src/shared/preview-channels.ts`.
- The Styles-panel property allowlist moved to `src/shared/style-props.ts`, with the renderer's `STYLE_PROP_META` `satisfies`-checked against it — a one-sided addition now fails typecheck.
- Two already-drifted preload payload types named and fixed (`SimElementPick` had lost `source: string | null`; `ProjectCreateResult` had lost `warning?`); stale `onMenuAction` doc comment corrected (8 → 14 actions).
- `registerPreviewIpc` (~400 lines) extracted from `src/main/index.ts` into `src/main/preview-ipc.ts` (index.ts: 1263 → 968 lines), collapsing the duplicated style-read/layers-read request-reply pattern into one `requestReply` helper.
- Preload's 24 copies of the subscribe/unsubscribe wrapper became one `on<T>()` factory (507 → 429 lines).
- New `test/style-tokens.mjs` unit test for the pure token re-resolution logic (security-relevant re-validation of island-supplied picks, previously only covered transitively).

Deliberately deferred to their own PRs: splitting `App.tsx`, `store.ts`, `ChatPanel.tsx`, and extracting `props.ts`'s shared source-file plumbing (tracked in `docs/TASKS.md`).

## Verification

- `bun run typecheck` clean after every commit.
- Unit tier green (the `devserver-net` test skipped — the CI sandbox refuses socket binds; the diff there is comment-only).
- Electron tier under `xvfb-run`: 55/56 pass; the `editor-search` failure reproduces identically at the base commit `5e71056`, so it is pre-existing.
- Preview-specific electron tests (`select-element`, `layers-panel`, `style-edit`, `comment-mode`, `annotations`, `prop-edit`, `text-edit`, `spawn-comment`, and more) re-run green after both the hardening and the refactor; permission/question tests (`chat-render`, `questions`) updated for `sessionKey` and green.
- `bun test/docs-links.mjs` passes; CLAUDE.md's architecture map updated for the new shared/main files.
